newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHENS BOURSE MAY TAP CBOE DERIVATIVES KNOW-HOW.
newsitem.headline: ATHENS BOURSE MAY TAP CBOE DERIVATIVES KNOW-HOW.

text.p: The Athens bourse, eyeing the launch of equity derivatives for some time, might benefit from the expertise and advice of developed markets like the Chicago Board of Options Exchange (CBOE).

"There has been no official request for assistance in the launch of derivatives but we would be interested in providing know-how if asked," William Barclay, CBOE Vice-President for strategic planning and international development told Reuters.
Having a derivatives capability would render the Athens stock exchange more competitive with international investors, allowing hedging opportunities, he said.
Barclay was speaking to Reuters on the fringe of an Athens conference on the modernisation of Greece's capital market.

"However, international investors know what a credible derivatives market looks like so it's better to do it right rather than rush it," said Barclay, who also heads the CBOE's technical assistance programme.
The CBOE provides customised know-how, feasibility studies and trains regulatory staff, helping other exchanges launch derivative products.

Earlier Barclay told the conference that by year-end 1995 options markets existed in 24 countries with almost 800 million contracts traded. At least eight countries were planning the creation of options markets.
Fueling this growth in the world of options was product innovation including surrogates, customisation, embedded options and option packages, he said.

Examples of surrogates, options designed to replicate returns of other instruments, included low-exercise-price- options (LEPOS) which are surrogates for cash positions and combinations -- doublets -- which act as futures.
Barclay said exchanges and issuers have also developed packaged options such as vertical spreads and buy-write packages for fans of covered call writing.

Asked whether U.S. derivatives markets were concerned by the approach of EMU and the launch of the euro, the common European currency, Barclay said those with currency products could face some pressure.

"The CBOE has no currency products that could be affected by EMU but other exchanges do. However, the real question is whether EMU is really going to happen," he told Reuters. --George Georgiopoulos, Intercontinental Hotel Newsroom +301 902.3666, ext. 6680
